findings.exact_text: The bridge fell away beneath him into the cloud sea, taking the rope's last anchor with it
findings.reason: Line was anchored to a trunk across the gap, and the bridge was torn loose; cutting the line from his harness leaves unclear how he swings free and lands, and where the line anchors.

findings.exact_text: The anchor trunk was failing, and the line was still looped around his harness.
findings.reason: Cutting the line is justified, but 'anchor trunk failing' conflicts with Nisa holding the line and with the bridge falling; the causal chain of what falls is muddled.

findings.exact_text: The gliders still waited where the old knotted trunk leaned
findings.reason: The line was unfastened from the trunk at the shore, and the glider's tilt was held by the line; the story never shows the gliders being secured, and Nisa's glider landing is never shown.

findings.exact_text: They didn't make it to the bridge.
findings.reason: They reach the bridge in the next paragraph, contradicting this statement; the camp location and bridge location also don't match the earlier route.
Nisa's ten-minute scouting limit is not tracked, and she returns with an urgent report; fine, but dusk and sun timing at landing is unestablished.

findings.exact_text: stayed a secret only he and Nisa knew
findings.reason: They bring home the journal and tag as proof, so calling the island a secret undercuts the ending's evidence and the promised local payoff.
A knife is not in the inventory authority; invented gear is minor but unsupported.
Odd, slightly awkward simile for a dense cloud wall.

findings.exact_text: and Arda swung free, and Nisa—guessing his move the instant he made it—leaned out and hauled, and his hand found her wrist, and her grip found him, and that was what saved him.
found the great root span torn loose in the wind
findings.reason: Spine says Arda swings Nisa across then cuts the line; the story has him cut the line while she hauls him, shifting the sacrifice logic.

findings.exact_text: "Race you to the bridge," he said.
findings.reason: Playful race tone after the quarrel is abrupt given the urgent corridor closing.

findings.exact_text: A length of bleached rope fiber
findings.reason: “A length of rope fiber” is an unnatural measure-and-material collocation; the visible object is naturally called a length of rope.

findings.exact_text: a cliff edge let him look out
findings.reason: This gives the cliff edge an awkward enabling role; ordinary English would place him at the vantage point and say he could look out.

findings.exact_text: and a storm-chest burst open—and the old signal kite
findings.reason: The repeated conjunction around the dash creates a clumsy attachment and momentarily obscures that the gust opens the chest before the kite rises.
Centimeters do not naturally measure the experience he hates here; “every second of it” is the idiomatic expression.
Using “thread” directly as the object of “flew” is overly compressed and spatially unclear; they fly through the threadlike corridor.

target_segments.source_text: The island itself was moving, sliding with terrible patience toward a wall of dense white cloud on the far side of the corridor, a wall that looked solid as a cliff made of milk.
A length of bleached rope fiber ran around the trunk, half-sunk into bark that had grown over it, knotted in a hitch he almost recognized—a guild-style anchor, but not any pattern currently taught.
On the far side of the bridge, a cliff edge let him look out over the whole interior, and what he saw stopped him cold: the old knots didn't stop.

A gust tore through the hollow, ripped the last canvas free, and a storm-chest burst open—and the old signal kite inside lifted, caught a thread of updraft, and climbed into the branches above them, snapping and wheeling like a live thing.
"Race you to the bridge," he said.
They didn't make it to the bridge.
The bridge never got the chance to carry them.

They came down through the mist-filled trees at a dead run and found the great root span torn loose in the wind, its far anchor ripped out, the whole thing sagging and thrashing above a drop into the cloud sea.
The anchor trunk was failing, and the line was still looped around his harness.
There was only one thing left to do, and he did it with his knife and hated every centimeter of it: he cut the line away from the sinking bridge.

The bridge fell away beneath him into the cloud sea, taking the rope's last anchor with it, and Arda swung free, and Nisa—guessing his move the instant he made it—leaned out and hauled, and his hand found her wrist, and her grip found him, and that was what saved him.
The shore, when they reached it, felt smaller than it had.
The gliders still waited where the old knotted trunk leaned, just as they'd left them.
They launched together off the sloping roots, catching the last updraft with the island sliding away under them, and flew the thread.

Then he took out the glider-tag and held it in his open palm, turning it so the unknown name caught the sunset, and wondered who had tied those knots, and whether they had ever made it home—while the island that had dissolved into the cloud wall stayed a secret only he and Nisa knew.
